$comment: Boundary-binary hashes of published toolkit releases — ADR 0006 D9.
The Server accepts a Sandbox whose boundary binaries match its own bundle OR
any single release listed here at or above `minimumVersion`. D9 takes a Server
newer than a running Sandbox as the normal case and requires the previous
Runner to keep working; equality against the Server's own bundle is a lockstep
check the system cannot hold, because a container outlives Server deploys.
A release is matched WHOLE. An entry that does not name every boundary binary
is skipped, and binaries from two different releases never combine into an
accepted toolkit: that combination was never published and never tested, and
its halves need not agree about the boundary they jointly enforce.
`minimumVersion` is not optional. Without it, accepting a set is a downgrade
path: an image pinned to a release with a known-bad toolkit would attest
cleanly for ever. Raise it whenever a release must stop being accepted. A file
without a readable floor is ignored entirely rather than read as no floor.
The checked-in releases bootstrap the compatibility window. At publish time
the trusted main workflow reconstructs the complete ledger from immutable Git
release tags, so every Server image contains every release up to its own and
runtime attestation requires no network lookup.
Entries are read defensively: a malformed file, a wrong shape, an unparsable
version or a value that is not 64 hex characters is ignored, and the Server
then accepts its own bundle alone — exactly the behaviour from before this
file existed. That is deliberate. This file can only ever WIDEN what is
accepted, so ignoring it cannot admit anything it should not, whereas failing
closed on a bad ledger would disable every project in the fleet.
While `releases` is empty the Server accepts its own bundle alone, which is
today's behaviour: the structure, the floor and the tests are in place, and
the compatibility this file describes begins when the build that publishes a
release starts writing its hashes here.
